# Sales Capacity and Quota Setting

Source: https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Most quota plans start from the board's number and divide it by headcount. Benchmarks suggest that leaves fewer than half of sellers at quota, while ramp times lengthen. This piece sets out a capacity model built from ramp, attainment and hiring dates, the gap it usually exposes, and how to record the quota decision so next year's plan can learn from this one.

Sales capacity is the revenue a team can realistically produce in a period, given who is in seat, how long new hires take to ramp and what share of quota sellers usually attain. Quota setting should start from that number and then reconcile it with the target, not the other way round. The Bridge Group's 2026 study of 158 B2B companies found 48% of account executives at quota, down from 51% in 2024, with average ramp time at 6.2 months, the longest in the study's history. A plan that ignores those two figures is a wish with a spreadsheet attached.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every annual plan contains a moment where a revenue target meets a sales team. In most firms of 20 to 500 people, that meeting is a division: the target divided by the number of sellers, adjusted a little for seniority and territory. The result is called a quota.

The division has the advantage of always balancing. Its disadvantage is that it encodes no evidence about what the team can carry. The quota becomes a statement of what the firm needs, and attainment becomes a measure of how far the need exceeded the capacity.

## What the benchmarks say about attainment

The evidence on attainment is consistent across sources, and it is not encouraging.

The Bridge Group's 2026 study of AE models and metrics, drawn from 158 B2B companies surveyed in the first half of 2026, found 48% of reps at quota, down from 51% in 2024. The median AE quota was $960,000 against median on-target earnings of $200,000, a quota-to-OTE ratio of 4.6, up from 4.2 in 2024. The firm's 2024 edition noted that median quota had grown at about 2% a year since 2012 while on-target earnings grew at more than 5%.

Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, built from 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, report that an average of 69% of reps were falling short in 2024, and that only 15% of sales teams had more than half their reps reach 80% of quota. They also found that average quota targets had been cut by 19%, and that 79% of reps would have missed at unchanged quotas.

KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures' 2024 private SaaS survey, of more than 100 companies, found quotas rose more than 10% in 2023 while expected attainment rose from about 70% to about 75%.

| Source | Sample | Attainment finding | What it implies for planning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bridge Group, 2026 | 158 B2B companies | 48% of AEs at quota, down from 51% | Plan on fewer than half the team hitting target |
| Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 | 4.2m opportunities, 530 companies | 69% of reps falling short on average | Quota cuts were needed mid-year in many teams |
| KeyBanc and Sapphire, 2024 | 100+ private SaaS firms | Quotas up 10%+; expected attainment about 75% | Firms raised targets and expectations together |

These are vendor and investor datasets weighted towards software, and definitions of attainment differ. They agree on the direction: a quota that most of the team misses is the norm, not the exception.

The ratios point the same way. When median quota rises faster than the evidence of what sellers close, attainment falls, and the difference is usually absorbed in one of three places: mid-year quota cuts, missed forecasts or seller turnover. Each of those costs more than an honest plan would have. A services firm faces the same arithmetic with billable targets in place of quota.

> If most of the team misses quota, the quota was a forecast error before it was a performance problem.

## Building capacity from the bottom

A capacity model answers one question: if the plan goes as expected, how much will the team sell? It needs four inputs per seller.

**Productive quota.** What a fully ramped seller in this role and segment has historically sold, not what they were asked to sell. Use the median of the last four quarters for ramped sellers, not the top performer.

**Ramp curve.** How many months a new hire takes to reach productive quota, and what share they deliver along the way. The Bridge Group's 6.2-month average is a reasonable default where the firm has no history of its own.

**Start date.** A seller hired in month seven of a twelve-month year cannot contribute a full year, and in most cases contributes little before the year ends.

**Attrition.** Some sellers will leave. Gartner's 2022 survey of 908 B2B sellers found 89% reporting burnout and 54% actively looking for another job. A plan that assumes everyone stays all year overstates capacity.

The table shows the effect of start date on first-year contribution, assuming, for illustration only, a six-month linear ramp.

| Start month | Months in seat this year | Approximate full-quota equivalent this year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January | 12 | About 75% |
| April | 9 | About 50% |
| July | 6 | About 25% |
| October | 3 | Under 10% |

Under these assumptions, a team of eight ramped sellers plus four hires spread through the year does not have twelve sellers' worth of capacity. It has roughly nine and a half, before attrition. That gap between headcount and capacity is the number most plans never write down. Apply an attrition assumption on top, and add back a ramp period for every replacement hire, and the figure usually falls further.

[*What is pipeline coverage?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-pipeline-coverage/) makes the parallel point for pipeline: the right ratio comes from your own win rate, not a rule of thumb. Capacity works the same way. Use your own ramp and attainment history once you have four quarters of it.

## Reconciling capacity with the target

The capacity model usually produces a number below the target. That is the useful moment, because the gap now has a size and the leadership team can choose how to close it.

There are five honest ways to close it. Each has a cost that belongs in the plan.

| Lever | What it does | What it costs | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hire earlier | Adds ramped months this year | Cash and management time now | Hire dates the plan depends on |
| Raise productivity | Lifts productive quota per seller | Enablement, tools or support roles | The specific change and its expected effect |
| Shift the mix | Moves effort to higher-yield segments or channels | Coverage elsewhere | Which accounts lose attention |
| Over-assign quota | Sum of quotas exceeds the target, as a buffer | Lower expected attainment and morale | The buffer size and why |
| Lower the target | Aligns the plan with capacity | A harder board conversation | The evidence presented |

Productivity is the lever most often assumed and least often evidenced. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently. A plan that counts on higher productive quota should name the change that removes work from sellers, and its expected effect, rather than assume the same people will simply sell more.

The dishonest way is to leave the gap unstated and distribute it across quotas. Gartner's 2022 survey found 67% of sellers saying their leadership was overly optimistic and disconnected from seller reality. A gap hidden in quotas is one reason that perception forms.

## Setting the individual number

Once the team number reconciles, individual quotas can be set. Three principles hold up across the evidence.

**Set quotas from territory potential, not from last year plus a percentage.** A territory with more accounts in the ideal customer profile can carry more. [*How to write an ICP*](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) covers how to define that profile so it can be counted.

**Design for the middle of the team.** Steenburgh and Ahearne's research, published in *Harvard Business Review* in 2012, found that sales forces divide into laggards, core performers and stars, and respond differently to plan design. Tiered targets motivated core performers; quarterly bonuses kept laggards on track, and moving them to annual bonuses was associated with a revenue drop of about 10%; caps on commission led stars to stop selling once they hit target.

**Change quotas mid-year only by a rule.** Ebsta and Pavilion's finding that average quotas were cut by 19% shows how common mid-year resets are. If resets happen, the rule for when and how should be written before the year starts, so a reset is a planned response rather than a negotiation.

Bridge Group's 2026 study also found that 38% of AEs now own renewal and expansion, nearly double the 2024 share. Where that is true, quota must state how renewal and new business are weighted, or sellers will choose the easier number.

## Recording the plan so next year can learn

The capacity plan is a commercial decision in the sense of [*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/): it is made once a year, defended to a board, and graded within twelve months. It is also one of the least often recorded with its reasoning.

The record needs six lines: the target, the capacity estimate with its assumptions, the gap, the levers chosen to close it, the owner, and the check date. At the year's end, write back the outcome: actual ramp, actual attainment, actual attrition. Over two or three cycles, the firm builds its own benchmarks, and the plan stops depending on borrowed ones.

This is also where forecasting and capacity meet. Part 23 of this series covered forecasting; a forecast that keeps missing in the same direction is often a capacity plan that was never reconciled.

Illustrative example: closing the gap in the open

Decision
:   Set the new-business target at the capacity estimate plus an 8% over-assignment buffer, and move two hires from the third quarter to the first.

Reason and owner
:   The bottom-up model, using the firm's own six-month ramp and last year's median attainment, came in below the board's first target. Agreed by the chief executive and the revenue lead; owned by the revenue lead.

What changed
:   The board saw the gap, the levers and the buffer. Actual ramp and attainment are written back at year end.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Model capacity before quota.** Ramp, start date, attainment and attrition decide what the team can carry.
- **State the gap.** The difference between capacity and target is a decision, not a rounding error.
- **Design for the core performers.** Tiered targets and regular bonuses matter more than the headline number.
- **Write the plan down with its assumptions.** Next year's plan should learn from this year's outcome.

Gateway card

### Before you publish quotas

- Productive quota per role taken from the median of ramped sellers
- A ramp curve from your own history, or a stated default
- Start dates for every planned hire
- An attrition assumption
- The gap between capacity and target written down, with the levers chosen
- A written rule for any mid-year quota change

Take this year's quota plan and add one line beneath it: the capacity estimate from ramp, start dates and last year's median attainment. If the two numbers differ, write down how the gap was closed and who agreed.
